strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile problem: predicting human response times under changing external stimuli. Combining task-trained neural representations with a policy-controlled evidence accumulator is a well-motivated approach that could provide useful cognitive structure.

The two-day experiment compares four stimulus schedules, with 36 retained participants. Evaluation across general, group, individual, and leave-one-participant-out settings provides useful perspectives on personalization and participant generalization.

The reported aggregate results consistently favor the hybrid agent over Pure DRL. MAPE decreases from 0.3034 to 0.2999 in the general setting and from 0.3037 to 0.2905 under LOPO. Feature comparisons support the arithmetic representation, and the reported training times of 4.42 versus 38.30 minutes suggest a potentially useful efficiency benefit.

Code and data availability are only promised. These omissions prevent reproduction and assessment of whether the implemented objective supports the principal claims.

The claimed explanation of cognition at individual stimulus frames is not established by response-time prediction. Many latent action trajectories can produce the same threshold-crossing time. The plotted trajectories therefore describe the fitted controller without demonstrating that participants use the inferred accumulation process. Nonzero inferred effects in the no-pressure group could also reflect correction of baseline prediction errors. Model-recovery experiments or controlled changes to within-trial stimulus timing would provide stronger evidence.

The main comparison does not isolate the contribution of the DDM. Pure DRL processes the whole stimulus and produces one adjustment, whereas the hybrid model processes sequential frames and actions. Temporal representation and decision structure therefore change together. A sequential neural baseline without the DDM, a stimulus-aware supervised predictor, and a fitted diffusion model with stimulus covariates are needed to establish the value of the proposed combination.

The predictive improvements are modest, and their reliability is unclear. The paper provides no uncertainty estimates or paired participant-level analysis for the MAPE differences, nor adequately documented repeated-seed results. The runtime comparison also lacks an operational convergence criterion and variability estimates. The evidence supports promising point estimates more strongly than robust superiority.

The evaluation pipeline is insufficiently documented. It is unclear which no-pressure observations train the baseline SVM and whether normalization, SVM fitting, and model selection occur entirely within each LOPO training fold. This leaves leakage risks unresolved rather than demonstrating leakage. Shuffled within-participant splits also assess interpolation across the study, not prospective prediction of later behavior.

Some behavioral conclusions exceed the statistical evidence. The reported significant response-time contrast is random versus none; this does not establish that random pressure outperforms every alternative. Likewise, nonsignificant accuracy differences do not establish that pressure leaves accuracy unaffected. With only 7–10 retained participants per group and unspecified criteria for excluding extreme outliers, sensitivity analyses would materially strengthen these conclusions.

Positioning against prior work needs greater precision. The suggestion that DDMs primarily support posterior estimation rather than future prediction is misleading: fitted generative diffusion models can make out-of-sample predictions. Although prior cognitive–neural and RL–DDM combinations are cited, the paper does not convincingly establish what additional predictive or explanatory capability its construction provides beyond those approaches.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: predicting human response times under changing external stimuli. Combining task-derived neural features with a controllable evidence-accumulation process is a well-motivated approach, and Figure 1 clearly communicates the overall architecture.

The two-day study provides repeated behavioral measurements across four stimulus conditions. Evaluating general, group, individual, and leave-one-participant-out settings is useful; the latter provides stronger evidence of generalization than shuffled trial splits alone.

The results provide preliminary evidence of practical value. Hybrid DRL achieves lower aggregate MAPE than Pure DRL in all four settings, including 0.2905 versus 0.3037 under leave-one-participant-out evaluation. The reported training times of 4.42 versus 38.30 minutes also suggest a potential computational benefit.
weaknesses: Essential methodological details are unavailable in the supplied manuscript. The referenced appendices S2–S6 are absent, leaving the RL algorithm and reward, evidence-update equations, diffusion noise, mapping from SVM predictions to DDM parameters, important hyperparameters, and adaptive stimulus rule insufficiently specified. Promised future code availability does not resolve these gaps, which prevent reproduction and assessment of the central method.

The comparison does not isolate the benefit of incorporating DDM. Pure DRL simultaneously removes DDM and replaces frame-level sequential decisions with a single trial-level action. Consequently, improvements could arise from temporal processing or the changed optimization problem. Comparisons with a matched sequential predictor, supervised response-time residual regression, and a fitted stimulus-dependent DDM are needed to establish the proposed combination's contribution.

The claimed cognitive interpretation exceeds the evidence. Observed response times do not uniquely identify within-trial evidence trajectories: multiple action sequences can produce the same threshold-crossing time. Agreement with aggregate behavioral trends therefore does not validate the inferred mechanism. Substantial nonzero 'time-pressure effect' trajectories also appear in the no-pressure condition (Figure 3p), suggesting that the controller can absorb baseline prediction error. Recovery experiments or predictions under independently varied stimulus schedules would provide more convincing validation.

The evaluation protocol needs clarification. It is unclear which no-pressure observations train the baseline SVMs and whether all human-data-dependent fitting, normalization, and tuning exclude held-out participants in each outer split. This leaves potential information leakage unresolved rather than demonstrated. Shuffled trial evaluations also do not establish forecasting performance on later trials or unfamiliar stimulus schedules.

The predictive gains over Pure DRL are modest, and their reliability is not quantified. For example, general-level MAPE changes from 0.3034 to 0.2999. Confidence intervals, paired participant-level comparisons, and reported variability across random seeds are needed to judge these differences. The training-efficiency claim similarly lacks a clearly specified convergence criterion and uncertainty.

The behavioral conclusions require more caution. Only 36 participants remain after exclusions, with seven in the random condition, and the criteria for removing three 'extreme outliers' are unspecified. Normalization against the first formal block uses a baseline already exposed to the assigned intervention and does not eliminate individual differences. The reported random-versus-none difference supports a limited comparison, not a demonstrated advantage over every other condition; nonsignificant accuracy differences likewise do not establish equivalence.

The distinction from prior work is insufficiently developed. The paper cites existing RL–DDM integration, including Pedersen et al. (2017), but offers limited technical comparison. The suggestion that DDM supports posterior estimation rather than prediction is not a sound general distinction. Novelty should be established around the specific learned stimulus-dependent modulation and its demonstrated benefits.

The two-day experiment provides substantial repeated-trial data from 36 analyzed participants across four stimulus conditions. Random assignment, a no-stimulus control, and measurements of response time, accuracy, attention, and anxiety provide useful empirical grounding.

It is also unclear which observations train the nominally pressure-free baseline and whether normalization and SVM fitting are repeated within each participant-held-out fold. These omissions prevent reproduction and verification of the evaluation protocol.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution. Pure DRL removes both the DDM and framewise sequential processing, so differences cannot be attributed specifically to the cognitive model. The SVM baseline omits stimulus information. Comparisons with stimulus-conditioned supervised response-time predictors, a sequential model receiving equivalent inputs, and a stimulus-conditioned DDM are needed to establish the value of the hybrid design.

The predictive gains lack uncertainty estimates. General-level MAPE improves only from 0.3034 to 0.2999, while the larger held-out-participant improvement is approximately 4.3% relative. Without paired participant-level uncertainty estimates or a documented repeated-seed evaluation, the reliability of these gains remains unclear. Likewise, the training-speed claim lacks an explicit convergence criterion and variability estimates.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Matching terminal response times does not identify the within-trial action trajectory: many trajectories can yield the same threshold-crossing time. Agreement between learned trajectories and behavioral patterns used for fitting therefore does not independently validate a cognitive mechanism. The behavioral conclusions need qualification. Although 50 people were recruited, only 36 were analyzed, with seven in the random condition; criteria for excluding three participants as extreme outliers are not supplied. The reported response-time post hoc evidence establishes a random-versus-none difference, rather than superiority over every other condition. Nonsignificant accuracy differences also do not establish that accuracy is unaffected. These limitations weaken the interpretation that random stimulation provides the best cognitive regulation.

The relationship to prior work is insufficiently developed. Earlier RL–DDM combinations are acknowledged in references 48–49, but the manuscript does not clearly establish its advance over these approaches or diffusion models with time-dependent drift or boundaries. The argument that conventional DDMs focus on posterior estimation overlooks their use as generative predictive models. The pure-DRL ablation changes the visual encoder, action scaling, and episode structure alongside removing DDM, confounding both accuracy and training-efficiency attribution. The additional DL+DDM controls are helpful, but matched sequential predictors and fitted diffusion models with stimulus-dependent parameters remain relevant comparisons. Tests with altered feedback timing or held-out intervention schedules would directly assess the stated objective. Positioning against existing RL–DDM work is also limited; conventional diffusion models can make prospective predictions.

The temporal alignment of CPC18 feedback needs clarification. Appendix A.11 describes alternative-outcome feedback as an input for predicting response time on each gambling trial. Such feedback ordinarily follows the decision. The paper must specify whether it uses preceding-trial feedback or another input available before the response; using same-trial post-response outcomes would undermine the interpretation as simulation of feedback-modulated decision time.

Statistical reporting does not establish the reliability of the gains sufficiently. Table 4 labels the empirical 2.5th and 97.5th error percentiles as a confidence interval, although these describe error dispersion rather than uncertainty in mean performance. The permutation-test sampling unit and treatment of repeated observations within participants are unspecified, and variability across training seeds is not reported. Participant-clustered paired uncertainty estimates would be more informative. Moreover, Table 8 does not establish a benefit from the risk encoder over its removal (permutation p = 0.677), weakening claims that every component is critical.

The PeerEdu evaluation requires a more appropriate metric analysis. Curiosity lies in [0,1], making MAPE unstable near zero and undefined at zero without an explicit convention. Figure 4 reports MAPE of 0.950, close to the error of 1.0 obtained by predicting zero for every strictly positive target. MAE or RMSE, explicit zero handling, and simple constant predictors are needed to assess the practical value of this extension.

Important reproduction details remain unclear despite the extensive appendix: the exact accumulation transition, sigmoid parameters, Brownian noise scale, action discount factor, and curiosity-specific dynamics are not fully specified. The paper should also state which observations train the no-pressure baseline and whether every human-data-trained stage is refitted within each evaluation split. A smaller reporting issue is the inconsistent participant count: Table 2 lists 50, Section 3 reports 44, and Appendix A.3.1 identifies 36 retained participants.

strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile problem: predicting human responses under changing environmental feedback. Combining task-solving representations, baseline response prediction, and an intervention-conditioned accumulation policy is a plausible and potentially useful modeling contribution.

The reported prediction gains are encouraging. In Table 1, numeric-input CogReact achieves MAPE 0.2703 versus 0.3052 for the strongest listed baseline, approximately an 11.4% relative reduction. The additional datasets and leave-one-participant-out experiments provide evidence beyond a single random train/test split.

The empirical investigation is substantial, including a newly collected dataset of 21,157 responses, four feedback conditions, multiple input representations, component ablations, and additional deep-learning-plus-DDM comparisons. These experiments make a serious effort to assess the proposed combination.
weaknesses: The central claim of explaining fine-grained cognitive mechanisms is insufficiently supported. Appendix A.7.1 constructs a noisy sigmoid trajectory from SVM predictions and uses an SVC probability as the decision boundary, without establishing why these quantities represent human evidence accumulation. Terminal response-time supervision permits many observationally equivalent trajectories. Figure 3 even shows nonzero 'time pressure effects' in the no-pressure group, suggesting that the policy also corrects baseline prediction errors. Matching response times and group trends therefore does not independently validate the inferred cognitive process.

The experiments do not isolate the importance of temporal stimulus structure. The mathematical task uses a fixed, repeating progress bar, and the best-performing version uses numeric feedback encoding. Controls that freeze or shuffle frames, remove feedback, or replace it with elapsed time would help establish what the model learns from the dynamic stimulus. Evaluation on previously unseen feedback schedules would directly test the paper's stated objective.

The ablations do not cleanly identify the source of improvement. The pure-DRL comparison changes the visual encoder, action scaling, and episode structure alongside removing the accumulation process, confounding both accuracy and training-time conclusions. Figure 11 is useful, but predicting DDM parameters is a different formulation from learning per-step corrections. Comparisons with a matched supervised residual model and fitted DDM/RL-DDM alternatives are needed. The characterization of conventional DDMs as primarily posterior estimators also understates their ability to generate trajectories and forward predictions.

The additional datasets leave important protocol questions unresolved. Appendix A.11 includes alternative-outcome feedback when predicting CPC18 response times without specifying whether feedback is lagged; using outcomes revealed after the current choice would invalidate the proposed prospective interpretation. For PeerEdu, converting curiosity magnitude into an accumulation stopping quantity through median binarization lacks a clear cognitive justification. MAPE on a target in [0,1] also requires explicit treatment of zero and near-zero values and complementary absolute-error metrics, especially with reported MAPE of 0.950.

Statistical uncertainty is not adequately established. Table 4 labels the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of individual errors as a 95% confidence interval; these do not quantify uncertainty in mean performance or model differences. The permutation tests do not specify how paired predictions and repeated observations within participants are handled, and variability across training seeds is not reported. Participant-level paired resampling would make the significance claims more convincing. Moreover, Table 8 does not support a critical contribution from the task encoder on CPC18: the permutation p-value against the unencoded hybrid is 0.677.

Reproduction requires clearer specification of the sigmoid trajectory, Brownian-noise scale, action coefficient lambda, and the strongest numeric-input CogReact variant. The paper should also state which observations train the purported no-feedback SVM baseline and confirm that every human-data-dependent stage is fitted within each training fold. Minor reporting corrections include consistently distinguishing 50 recruited, 44 main-study, and 36 retained participants, and correcting the boundary notation in A.7.5. Overall, the predictive merits are substantive, but the mechanistic and evaluation concerns make weak rejection the more appropriate recommendation.
